{{DISPLAYTITLE:Inductive types and recursors}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Building things from constructors|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Induction, as the machine sees it}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Apart from universes, function types and quotient types, which are built in, every type in
Lean is an '''inductive type''' or is defined in terms of universes, functions and inductive
types.<ref name="refman-ind">''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.34.0, lean-lang.org,
2026, section 4.4, "Inductive Types".
https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/</ref> The
natural numbers, lists, pairs, conjunction and disjunction, equality and the existential
quantifier are all inductive types. An inductive type is given by its constructors, and from
them Lean derives one more constant, the '''recursor''', which is at once the type's induction
principle and its means of primitive recursion. This page describes what an inductive
definition adds to Lean's environment, its table of definitions and theorems; the reduction
rule that makes recursors compute; the strict positivity condition and why it is needed; and,
briefly, indexed, mutual and nested types.

== What a definition adds ==

An inductive definition names a '''type constructor''' and a list of '''constructors''':

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print Nat
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive Nat : Type
number of parameters: 0
constructors:
Nat.zero : Nat
Nat.succ : Nat → Nat
</pre>

The type constructor <code>Nat</code>, the constructors <code>Nat.zero</code> and
<code>Nat.succ</code>, and the recursor <code>Nat.rec</code> are new constants with no
defining term: Lean adds them as axiomatic constants.<ref name="carneiro2019">Mario
Carneiro, ''The Type Theory of Lean'', MSc thesis, Carnegie Mellon University, 2019.
https://github.com/digama0/lean-type-theory/releases/tag/v1.0</ref> The
recursor in particular has a function type but is primitive, and cannot be defined using
<code>fun</code>.<ref name="refman-ind" />
What makes them more than arbitrary axioms is that their types are computed from the
definition by a fixed scheme, and that the definition must pass checks, described below,
which guarantee that adding them cannot make the logic inconsistent. The checks are
conservative: some harmless definitions are rejected too.<ref name="refman-ind" />

Every other property of the type is derived from the recursor. Injectivity of the
constructors, the fact that distinct constructors give distinct values, case analysis and
structural recursion are theorems and definitions built from <code>Nat.rec</code>, not
further primitives.<ref name="refman-ind" />

== The recursor ==

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check Nat.rec
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 prints

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Nat.rec.{u} {motive : Nat → Sort u} (zero : motive Nat.zero) (succ : (n : Nat) → motive n → motive n.succ) (t : Nat) :
  motive t
</pre>

The arguments have standard names.<ref name="refman-ind" /><ref name="carneiro2019" />

* The '''motive''' is a family of types indexed by the inductive type, <code>motive : Nat → Sort u</code>. It says what is being constructed or proved for each number.
* There is one '''minor premise''' per constructor. The one for <code>zero</code> is a value of <code>motive zero</code>. The one for <code>succ</code> takes <code>n</code> and a value of <code>motive n</code>, the result for the recursive argument, and returns a value of <code>motive (n + 1)</code>.
* The '''major premise''' <code>t</code> is the value the recursion runs on, and the result has type <code>motive t</code>.

Because the motive may land in any universe <code>Sort u</code>, the same constant does two
jobs. With a motive into <code>Prop</code>, <code>Nat.rec</code> is mathematical induction:
the minor premises are the base case and the induction step. With a motive into
<code>Type</code>, it is primitive recursion. Both uses below are checked by the same rule:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def double (n : Nat) : Nat :=
  Nat.rec (motive := fun _ => Nat) 0 (fun _ ih => ih + 2) n

#reduce double 3

theorem zero_add' (n : Nat) : 0 + n = n :=
  Nat.rec (motive := fun k => 0 + k = k) rfl (fun _ ih => congrArg Nat.succ ih) n
</pre>

<code>#reduce double 3</code> prints <code>6</code>. In general the recursor's type is
determined by the constructors alone: each constructor contributes a minor premise that
assumes the motive for each of its recursive arguments.<ref name="carneiro2019" /> Dybjer
gave a general formulation of this idea for Martin-Löf's type theory, in which the
elimination and equality rules of a new type are derived from its formation and introduction
rules, and Lean's treatment of inductive types is based on his.<ref name="lean4lean">Mario Carneiro, "Lean4Lean: Verifying a
Typechecker for Lean, in Lean", in ''31st International Conference on Types for Proofs and
Programs (TYPES 2025)'', LIPIcs vol. 384, pp. 2:1–2:23, 2026.
https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.TYPES.2025.2 (read in the version arXiv:2403.14064v2)</ref><ref name="dybjer1994">Peter Dybjer, "Inductive families", ''Formal Aspects of
Computing'' 6(4), 1994, pp. 440–465. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01211308</ref>

Lean's core has recursors but no pattern matching and no recursive definitions. Pattern
matching and recursion in source text are compiled into uses of the recursor, so the
recursor is also what guarantees that recursive functions terminate; how that is done is the
subject of [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Structural and well-founded recursion|Structural and well-founded recursion]].

== Iota reduction ==

A recursor applied to a constructor reduces to the corresponding minor premise, applied to
the constructor's arguments. This is
'''iota reduction''', and it is part of definitional equality. For <code>Nat</code> the two
rules are

:<math>\mathrm{Nat.rec}\;C\;z\;s\;\mathrm{zero} \equiv z \qquad \mathrm{Nat.rec}\;C\;z\;s\;(\mathrm{succ}\;n) \equiv s\;n\;(\mathrm{Nat.rec}\;C\;z\;s\;n)</math>

When a constructor has recursive arguments, the minor premise receives the recursor applied
to them, which is how recursion proceeds.<ref name="refman-ind" /><ref name="carneiro2019" />
Both rules hold by <code>rfl</code>, with the step function and the starting value left as
variables:

<pre class="lean lean-cont" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example (z : Nat) (s : Nat → Nat → Nat) :
    Nat.rec (motive := fun _ => Nat) z s 0 = z := rfl

example (z : Nat) (s : Nat → Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) :
    Nat.rec (motive := fun _ => Nat) z s (n + 1)
      = s n (Nat.rec (motive := fun _ => Nat) z s n) := rfl
</pre>

The second example is stated with <code>n + 1</code>, which is definitionally equal to
<code>Nat.succ n</code>. Iota
reduction is the computational content of an inductive type. Without it the recursor would
be an axiom stating that induction holds; with it, <code>double 3</code> is
<code>6</code> by calculation, and a proof by <code>rfl</code> is a computation the Lean kernel
carries out. See [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Definitional equality|Definitional equality]].

== Strict positivity ==

Not every list of constructors is acceptable. Every occurrence of the type being defined in
the type of a constructor argument must be '''strictly positive''': it may not appear to the
left of an arrow, however deeply nested, and it may appear as an argument only of the type
constructor of another inductive type.<ref name="refman-ind" /> The following definition
breaks the rule, because <code>Liar</code> appears as the domain of a function argument:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive Liar where
  | mk : (Liar → False) → Liar
</pre>

Lean 4.34.1 rejects it with a message marked <code>(kernel)</code>: the first argument of <code>'Liar.mk'</code>
has a non positive occurrence of the datatypes being declared.

The message comes from Lean's kernel, not the elaborator: the check is part of the trusted
core.

The reason is that such a type would prove <code>False</code>. If <code>Liar</code> existed,
its constructor would give <code>mk : (Liar → False) → Liar</code>, and case analysis on its
one constructor would give a function <code>unmk : Liar → (Liar → False)</code> that returns
the function a value was built from. Those two functions are all that is needed:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example (L : Type) (mk : (L → False) → L) (unmk : L → L → False) : False :=
  let notL : L → False := fun l => unmk l l
  notL (mk notL)
</pre>

Lean accepts this. <code>notL</code> applies a value to itself, as in Russell's paradox, and
feeding it its own image under <code>mk</code> yields a proof of <code>False</code> with no
induction at all. Strict positivity excludes every definition of this shape. Its exclusion of
an occurrence nested under an arbitrary function, as in
<code>f (Fix f) → Fix f</code> for a parameter <code>f</code>, is needed because a suitable
<code>f</code> would rebuild the same circularity.<ref name="refman-ind" /> Dybjer's criteria
for well-formed inductive families are likewise stated for strictly positive
definitions.<ref name="dybjer1994" />

Other checks concern universes: the arguments of a constructor must live in universes no
larger than that of the type being defined, except that a type in <code>Prop</code> may take
arguments from any universe. A type in <code>Prop</code> also has a restricted recursor whose motive can only be
a proposition, unless it has at most one constructor whose arguments are all propositions,
parameters or indices; this is '''subsingleton elimination''', treated on
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination|Proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination]].<ref name="refman-ind" />

== Indexed families ==

A type constructor may take two kinds of argument. '''Parameters''' are fixed across the whole
definition. '''Indices''' may differ from one constructor to another, so an indexed
definition defines a whole family of types at once, each member with its own
constructors.<ref name="refman-ind" /> Equality is the leading example:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print Eq
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive Eq.{u_1} : {α : Sort u_1} → α → α → Prop
number of parameters: 2
constructors:
Eq.refl : ∀ {α : Sort u_1} (a : α), a = a
</pre>

The type <code>α</code> and the left-hand side <code>a</code> are parameters; the right-hand
side is an index. There is one constructor, and it produces only <code>a = a</code>. The
family <code>a = b</code> is therefore inhabited exactly when <code>b</code> is
<code>a</code>, and its recursor, <code>Eq.rec</code>, is the principle of substituting equals
for equals; [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Propositional equality|Propositional equality]] follows it further.

A second example is a list whose length is part of its type:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : Nat → Type u where
  | nil : Vect α 0
  | cons : α → Vect α n → Vect α (n + 1)

def Vect.head : Vect α (n + 1) → α
  | cons a _ => a

#eval (Vect.cons 1 (Vect.cons 2 Vect.nil)).head
#check Vect.rec
</pre>

The evaluation prints <code>1</code>. <code>Vect.head</code> needs no case for
<code>nil</code>: an argument of type <code>Vect α (n + 1)</code> cannot be <code>nil</code>,
whose index is 0, and the pattern-match compiler uses the index to see this. The recursor's
motive now takes the index as well as the value,

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Vect.rec.{u_1, u} {α : Type u} {motive : (a : Nat) → Vect α a → Sort u_1} (nil : motive 0 Vect.nil)
  (cons : {n : Nat} → (a : α) → (a_1 : Vect α n) → motive n a_1 → motive (n + 1) (Vect.cons a a_1)) {a✝ : Nat}
  (t : Vect α a✝) : motive a✝ t
</pre>

and each minor premise fixes the index that its constructor produces. Indexed definitions of
this kind are Dybjer's '''inductive families'''.<ref name="dybjer1994" />

== Mutual and nested types ==

Several types may be defined together in a <code>mutual</code> block, each constructor
referring to any of them; the predicates "even" and "odd" on the natural numbers are a
standard case. The recursor of a mutual group takes one motive per type and one minor
premise per constructor of every type in the group.<ref name="refman-ind" />

A '''nested''' type is one in which the type being defined occurs as an argument of another
inductive type, as in a tree whose node holds a list of subtrees:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive Tree (α : Type) where
  | node : α → List (Tree α) → Tree α

#check @Tree.rec
</pre>

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
@Tree.rec : {α : Type} →
  {motive_1 : Tree α → Sort u_1} →
    {motive_2 : List (Tree α) → Sort u_1} →
      ((a : α) → (a_1 : List (Tree α)) → motive_2 a_1 → motive_1 (Tree.node a a_1)) →
        motive_2 [] →
          ((head : Tree α) → (tail : List (Tree α)) → motive_1 head → motive_2 tail → motive_2 (head :: tail)) →
            (t : Tree α) → motive_1 t
</pre>

The recursor has a second motive, for lists of trees, with minor premises for the empty list
and for a list cell. It has the shape of the recursor of a mutual pair of types, trees and
lists of trees, because that is how Lean's kernel justifies a nested type: it translates the
nested definition into a mutual one and accepts the original only if the translation
succeeds.<ref name="refman-ind" /> Direct support for nested types is one of the extensions of
the Lean 4 kernel over its predecessor, and Carneiro identifies it, with eta for structures,
as one of the two extensions that change the theory rather than abbreviate it.<ref name="lean4lean" />

== Where the scheme comes from ==

In the pure Calculus of Constructions, data and predicates could be represented by
higher-order quantification, an encoding that was inefficient as a program and weak as a
logic; the calculus was therefore extended with a primitive notion of inductive
definition.<ref name="pm1993">Christine Paulin-Mohring, "Inductive definitions in the
system Coq: rules and properties", in ''Typed Lambda Calculi and Applications'' (TLCA 1993),
Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Springer, 1993, pp. 328–345.
https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0037116</ref> The result, the Calculus of Inductive
Constructions, is the theory Lean was based on when the project began in 2013.<ref name="lean4">Leonardo de
Moura and Sebastian Ullrich, "The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language (System
Description)", in ''Automated Deduction – CADE 28'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science,
Springer, 2021, pp. 625–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37</ref> Lean's
presentation differs visibly from Coq's here: Coq's core uses primitive
<code>fix</code> and <code>match</code>, with a check that each recursive call is made on a
component produced by a <code>match</code>, while Lean's core has only recursors, and
definitions written with recursion and matching are compiled into them before the Lean kernel
sees them.<ref name="carneiro2019" /> The history is told on
[[Lean theorem prover/History/The Calculus of Constructions|The Calculus of Constructions]].
